I remember buying this game 10 years ago. I was either 13 or 14 and this game looked awesome, a real "HACK THE WORLD" kind of experience, but in a more realistic light than WatchDogs. When I played it then, it was pretty overwhelming, throwing unfamiliar commands and phrases to my tiny Windows user brain.

It was only when I was around a Junior or Senior in High School that I finally beat the game. It was beautiful, from the badass music to the witty humor hidden in text files; it was a peek into a world I wanted to be a part of.

Immediately after, I began my Computer Science degree in College. I realized that all the phrases the game was throwing at me (SSH, FTP, SMTP etc.) were all real life protocols. It was thanks to this game that I had a head start in my studies, and it was the perfect foundation for my internal computer networking knowledge-base. 

And here I am now, getting my Masters degree in Cyber Security. I use Linux every day, built my own computers and run my own home lab. I've just completed Hacknet, done everything I can do. From Entropy to /el, I've seen everything the base game has to offer.

Would I say it's a realistic hacking simulator? God no, but it's fun and a great entry point for the subject.

Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very cult genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. 

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc. 

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.  

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it. 

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into. 

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into. 

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look ar ound some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

While this game is being sold as a "hacking simulator", a debate will likely rage about what exactly it simulates. In either case, it comes suspiciously close to being a realistic simulation of hacking. So close, in fact, I'm left wondering why the dev didn't go the extra yards to make it inarguably so (maybe something he can shoot for in the future). Realism nit-picking aside, this game is full of very realistic nods to hacker and IRC culture, and in broad strokes, represents some of what goes on in actual exploits. While the experience of compromising systems is streamlined for the sake of keeping it an actual game (again, is it a puzzle game or a simulator?), in that "push a button, get bacon" sort of way you see in "hacker" movies, there was still much in the game that reminded me of taking the OSCP (for those who know my pain, you will find much in each mission to make you smile in that corpse-like rictus you had while laughing at emails and files during enumeration pratice in the Offsec lab).

After a while, I realized I was playing not so much because of the faux-hacking experience, but because there was a rather compelling story unfolding. Can't pick that apart without spoiling it, so I'll critique the gameplay instead (positives first):

[b]Pros:[/b]
This game is hilarious in a sick, twisted way. References to chan and IRC culture litter the storyline. While the majority of gameplay involves limited exploit combinations, there are moments where you don't know what the f**k is going on, and you have to think fast to avert a crisis. If you're into security culture, you'll find your intuition meshes well with the challenges, and you can improv what to do most of the time. It's like a Drunk History version of real hacking, so it's probably an ideal game to play while you're drunk.

People with zero knowledge of hacker culture or basic unix commands and quad notation will walk away familiar with all of the above.

The game is cheap, so whether you enjoy the simplistic, repetitive nature of the "hacking" it simulates, you won't regret the purchase, because it will entertain you regardless. The story itself is worth the price, and the way the story is told using the genre is clever.

If you liked TIS-100 (and I'm a recovering TIS-addict) you'll appreciate this for some of the same reasons, but the games aren't identical by a long shot. In fact, that would be the one constructive criticism I'd like both devs of these two games to hear: if TIS-100 had the narrative of Hacknet, and Hacknet had the coding fatures and complexity of TIS-100, you'd have a seriously ground breaking game on your hands, guys.

[i]Maybe the two of you should consider a collab or something...[/i]

[b]Cons:[/b]

Pushing buttons to get bacon gets fairly boring after a while, and the game loses some of its puzzle quality attributes as a result of the limited attack combinations, and the lack of customization or tweaking of exploits and tactics that is the real joy of hacking. If this was never going to be a hacking game, and more of a puzzle game, I wanted to see a complexity progression throughout, instead of a chaotic difficulty plataeu. 

[b]Also, why write so many missions for lelzsec, but make it so easy to permanently lose your chance to access them -- it was like a quarter of the game just gets skipped automagically because there isn't a clear choice presented to the player that an alternate path exists![/b]

Each mission certainly could have involved more manual hacks to achieve both realism and puzzle difficulty, but this would require adding more OS commands to the game, or a limited scripting engine of some sort. It couldn't have been that hard to add a mission where the solution was to exploit weak service permissions, tampering with programs launched by the OS at boot. Perhaps telling the print spooler to reset the system's admin password by re-writing it to launch a file with a "passwd" command in it, or to add a user account with "admin" privileges, something along these lines. A phishing mission, or getting a target to open an email and trigger a malicious trojan embedded in a PDF file would have been fun. These kinds of scenarios would require no "hacking tools", and might actually require the player to struggle. I'd rather struggle than push "exploit" over and over, my only real enemy being the trace timer.

To do this would require more system commands like "touch", privileges to edit, the ability to create files, maybe a basic word processor and the ability to write emails (instead of just reply... to some of them). All we had to work with were pre-existing files, a "replace" command that replaces lines and is too cumbersome, and no manner of scripting available. No complex chains of commands, no writing or editing code beyond some HTML (so I can change "chicken" to "c**ks", but that's not really hacking as much as being a d**k).

Once you get to that long slog of a valley mid-game, it stops feeling like hacking AND puzzle solving, and starts to feel more like grinding mobs in an MMO to get to the next bit of storyline. Each player will have more or less patience for that experience. Exploit tactics become routine too quickly, and the difficulty drops off.

[b]OVERALL[/b]:
Short game. In 20 hours you can play through twice and get all the achievements, and you compulsively will, despite the bugs that might force you to start a new game because something is glitched and can't recover [though the developer is working hard to patch all these, props to him]. There are enough Easter Eggs and humorous logs to make you anxious that you missed some the first time. More like an interactive novel for hackers than a puzzle game or simulator, but with elements of both; you will feel haunted putting together what your *actual* role in the missions might have been, and to what extent the Ayy Lmaos were involved. 

For $8-ish, I felt like I got more than I paid for and told my friends to play it for the lulz.

Hacknet is an absolute gem of a game. 

[b]TLDR: [/b]While people already familiar with using *nix or general programing principles may find this game not too deep or challenging, it offers a well thought out narrative, with fun game mechanics and excels at teaching you about computer essentials without you even realizing it. 


[b]More thoughts:[/b] 

While this game isn't perfect, I would still reccomend it to anyone who has even a remote interest in computers. Even if you only want to feel like a hacker in a movie, that game gives you that feeling. If you want to learn more about the general concepts of computer-, program-, and network-architecture, this game is a great launching-point, before you start reading more "serious" or conventional literature on the subject. 

Now, the mechanics are pretty straight-forward. You gain various programs through completing quests, which, in turn, can be used to bypass more complex security. You also gain the ability to run commands through other computers, allowing you, for example, to pretty much emulate a DDOS attack. Timing is also important, so be ready to type "dc" + [enter] if you're being tracked. AAAAAAAAANNNNNNDDDDDD............

.....
.....
.....

that's pretty much it when it comes to mechanics. The rest is working your way through systems full of mostly text-files, a lot of them taken from bash.org (hilarious quotes from internet chats, NSFW, but great!), and a lot of fun easter-eggs for nerds and fans of "hacker-culture" as it has been created by Hollywood. There even are multiple references to the movie "Hackers", a must see in my opinion. ;)

Now, the mechanics got old after not too long (a good 8 hours), mainly due to you unlocking a lot of the tools that you need pretty quickly. I'll talk more about overall gameplay features in just a moment. 

The narrative is fun, well paced, and interwoven well with the gameplay mechanics. I won't spoil anything, just watch the trailer and you get the general premise. 

The overall game is simplified, to allow people without prior experience to enjoy it, but encourages experimentation and exploration of what you can do, giving you plenty of examples and hints along the way to teach you, without you even realizing it, a lot about how your system works. Absolutely amazing!

Concerning the lack of gameplay features, the dev is amazing. Yup, one dev. And he's already said that he wants to implement multiplayer. If that happens, this will become one of the best games out there. Period. Plus he wants to continue to push content for the game. Not to mention, that the community as a whole is awesome and really suportive for newcomers. 

In its current state, it's well worth the price its asking for. As the dev continues to push more content, the game will continue to expand and improve. 

Please support this game, as its honestly trying to be different and fun, without a lot of the backstabbing and abusive tactics emplyed by all too many triple AAA studios/publishers. I can guarantee, you'll have a blast playing this!

I would just like to point towards the roadmap the dev has for 2016, which includes multiplayer and steam-workshop integration for custom missions throughout various points this year. http://steamcommunity.com/games/365450/announcements/detail/955130645658936382

An interesting mix between Uplink and Street Hacker, for the price of ~10 USD is definitely worth checking out.

The game is pretty fun, some things require attention to detail and logical thinking, and the humor is pretty good!

However, the game launched with a very bad bug which might make your save useless: if you try to make two missions at a time, you won't be able to complete the first one. This can simply kill your save.

The biggest difference here is being able to use both a GUI and a Console - which is good news.

This doesn't detract from the enjoyment of the game, of course. But it does dissapoint if you expected anything more than that.

I haven't finished the game yet, due to the bug that probably broke my savegame. But about the plot: it's decently intriguing and will make you want to uncover all the secrets, as a hacking game should.

So even though I ended up pretty disappointed - it's 2015, yet there's little news here. Even Street Hacker, which is a decade old and terribly programmed, had deeper features; and Uplink had a more compelling gameplay and story - there's still some fun to be had and some jokes/moments actually made me laugh or smile. 
I do recommend waiting for a patch before playing it, though. So rush it on your own risk. :)

[h3]Accurate Hacking Simulator?[/h3]

I was not exposed to a lot of hacking in games, maybe just a bit in Sleeping Dogs, or Cyberpunk 2077. While other games focus purely on hacking vibes, those tend to ignore the actual process. And Hacknet pays much more attention to the realistic aspect of the game.

Of course, to me it looks like huge oversimplification, but that was made as a game, right? It was made to be simple, fun and accessible. And it never felt like I am working, it felt like I am playing a game and having a good time. So while not being accurate, it nails the realistic hacking experience to enough extent. 

[h3]Handholding or Exploration?[/h3]

The first 60% to 70% percent of the game felt like a tutorial. Fun, with a lot of stories and action, but with a huge sense that I am playing in a sandbox. Everything is pretty safe, and you get what you need to do right from the email, so you need to execute specific steps without much investigation. Yes, you need to look for something specific, but it is usually very algorithmic and follows the same steps. 

So, this feels like handholding to me, and having to "detective" part to it, where you just don't know where to look at and have to think and explore. 

But! There are endgame quests, such as the main story line or Project Junebug quest. Those actually did things perfectly as I have wanted. There is more to reading, investigating, searching and connecting pieces of information together. This was perfect. 

Example: usually it would be "find a (file / password / IP) or edit / remove something. Here is the server.". That is straightforward. 

Project Junebug: Here is the name of the person. Kill him. 

You see what I mean? That is perfect example of what I wanted this game to be. And it eventually has things that appeal to me! So, overall, great experience. Right?

[h3]A bit of so-so moments[/h3]

Just one. The game has netMap, a graph that displays the machines you have connected to. And the graph grows, and there is less and less space, it all  becomes cluttered at some point. And there is no way to clean it up, resize, organize or alter. And this is sad a bit, because the missions that I liked involve a lot of research, but the research progress was hevily impacted by overall messy navigation system. 

But it's a minor thing. What else?


[h3]The Easter Eggs and Secrets[/h3]

While the big part of the game feels like a tutorial, it has a lot of things to explore. Jokes and memes, hidden quests with high rewards - it's all there. So if you want, you can take much more from the game than it offers at a first sight.

Like in some RPGs you can even get overpowered pretty early - if you follow some clues in the game, you can get CLOCK.EXE, which makes game itself hacked. Things that are hidden and require exploration definitely cool here.

[h3]The Music[/h3]

I pay a lot of attention to game OSTs, it makes me love the game more if the music resonates with me. And back in 2017 when I have bought the game, I learned about Hacknet from Remi (The Algorithm) - one of the musicians behind the OST, and I bought it. So, to me the OST is perfectly fitting the game. Just very neat, I thought. Until the final mission.

I have three examples of getting goosebumps from the music in the game:
1. One optional boss fight in Baldur's Gate 3
2. Expedition 33 in various places.

And... Yeah, the final mission of Hacknet! Putting [spoiler]Carpenter Brut's Roller Mobster[/spoiler], one of my favorite synthwave / darksynth tracks ever made me freeze for a minute in awe. And then realize that time is ticking and I need to do everything fast. Perfect sense of adrenaline. Great choice for OST!

[h3]Really solid hacking-lite experience[/h3]

Overall, I liked this game. Relatively short, but never gets dull. And I have not even touched the DLC yet - and it has 97% positive rating! So, while the main game is over for me, I will get to Labyrinths in future to feel this enjoyment again.

[h1]Surprisingly good.[/h1]
If you have ever played Uplink, you have a fair idea of what is going on in the world of Hacknet: as an aspiring hacker, you enter the murky world, learn through contracts and eventually achieve your goals.

Featuring a well-written story, superbly appropriate soundtrack and a smooth and intuitive interface, Hacknet does well to draw you in and recreate the feeling of system reconnaissance with a view to breaching. While I feel the work is intended to be done mostly through CLI with the various commands provided, those of a less technical mind can still use the GUI for most functions (not all, actually hacking in requires the CLI and the various tools needed to gain access), removing that as a potential barrier to entry. The game also does very well in recreating an intense atmosphere, mostly through the ticking tracer: as the time ticks down it does place some stress on you as you try to breach, grab whatever information you came for, wipe your traces and disconnect again - before the clock hits 0.

The Labyrinths DLC is outstanding and virtually a mandatory purchase along with the base game. While in reality it is a standalone "campaign", it diverges radically from the base game with its mission structure, the interaction with contracts as well as the story. In general, DLC is a nice to have rather than a must have, but in this case Labyrinths is an almost integral part of the experience.

You will find it easier (although it is certainly not a requirement) if you have some Linux/Unix skills before starting. All can be done through the GUI provided, but the experience is best if you operate through the CLI - for which it is best to understand and be able to use commands such as ls, cat, rm, mv and so on. Its not a full implementation of Linux (e.g. you cannot remove filename.* from a directory - you either need to remove each individually or do rm *; autocomplete also does not work past the first level of directory structure) but it is close enough to immerse the player; it is a minor point anyway. I would also suggest either keeping a notepad open on another screen, or having pen and paper close to hand: it will make it easier to keep track of IPs, usernames/passwords, files and so on. Attention to detail is important and can often be the difference between a successful hack and an unsuccessful one.

It is a unique game and if the concept of a hacking "simulator" appeals to you, or if you have enjoyed Uplink in the past - do not miss out on Hacknet.

I’m not entirely sure what to think about this game. I feel like this game had the potential to be a lot more interesting than it turned out to be. I did have fun with this game and thought some of the missions were interesting. But, I can’t really figure out what this game is trying to be and I came away with the feeling that this game isn’t really finished. 

In terms of hacking and the operating system, it’s fairly weak and, at times, frustrating. The hacking programs you run are basically magic in terms of how powerful they are. They work on anything and require no modification based on the target. The challenge comes from managing your bizarre computer’s memory system and timing attacks to avoid the hollywood-style ‘tracing’. The simplified hacking mechanics aren’t a bad thing, I think. Real hacking elements would make the game extremely complicated, tedious, and boring. 

But, that aside, there are weird limitations on what you can do and what exists in the world. The operating system commands you run are unix-based, but quickly get frustrating to use for anyone familiar with *nix command lines. Autocompletion and wildcards are inconsistent (‘rm *’ works but not ‘rm file_*’). There is no cp (copy), mkdir, rmdir, rsync, or recursion-supported operations. There isn’t even a text editor of any kind, opting for a bizarre ‘replace’ to replace strings in a given file. This just causes more frustration than anything as folders become cluttered and basic OS actions can't be done.

As for the world, hacking into servers and snooping around is fun… to a point. You can read other people’s emails, deface websites, and steal files, which is fun! Then you realize that most of the files you discover are copy-pasted bash.org quotes or filler files which you can’t do anything with. Also, you’re strongly told early on to remove the log files you leave behind when hacking a server, but I’ve yet to find an instance where there are any consequences for not doing so outside of one mission. Finally, and probably my biggest problem, is that you’re pretty much the only active user on the entire internet. You’ll never accidentally encounter another hacker when breaking into a server and you’ll (with one exception) never find log files or evidence of dynamic activity from anyone else on the internet. The world is completely static, apart from a few scripted events. Maybe if there were random encounters or events with other hackers where both of you have the ability to hack each other and other servers, the world wouldn’t feel so static and empty and it would keep you on your toes a bit more. 

The investigation and puzzle aspects of the game are interesting. But, the large number of typos,  grammar mistakes (not sure if these two are intentional or not), and questionable writing can be distracting and confusing. That said, I still had fun. There are times where the missions can be very interesting and even disturbing. And, occasionally, there are times where you have to be clever to solve a puzzle or find a missing piece of information. But, those events are far and few in between. Most of the ‘contracts’ start to feel tedious pretty quickly.

I hate that there is no option inbetween the thumbs up and down, because I think the game is still fun. But, comparing how much I liked to how much I didn’t like, I have to give it a thumbs down. This game has great ideas, it just hasn’t fleshed them out enough.

Hacknet is a great intro to Unix command line interface.  There are lots of basic command line tutorials out there but to build muscle memory, you need to use commands like cd (change directory) and ls (list content) over a 100 times.  However who wants to change directory and list directory content over 100 times?  Thus most tutorials will let you practice a command couple times then move on--not building muscle memory.  Hacknet is the solution! In Hacknet you will connect to multiple computers on the net, traversing the file system via the command line and it before you know it you will build muscle memory.  The story is well written and compelling enough that typing the same commands over and over (grinding) to "flip the page" of the story is worth it.

If you are doing this for just the learning purposes--many realistic hacking game reviews recommend Hacknet as a prerequisite.  I recommend getting the Labyrinth expansion because it add new tools to learn.  When no new tools or commands are offered, start the Labyrinth expansion mission, The Kaguya Trials--start Labyrinth missions early rather than later.  Hacknet stops introducing new concepts about mid way and the Labyrinth expansion brings the learning back.   Mid Labyrinth missions, decide when you practiced enough and stop playing.

I love this game!!! As a game developer and compsci student, I was THOROUGHLY impressed by this game! I love the concept, the execution is very clever (the RAM limitation was brilliant!), and at one point you even get hit by an opponent and lose your UI and must do everything through cmd, and it's just... IT'S BRILLIANT, OKAY?! I love this so much, and I am super curious where the plot is going!

I have nearly 100% the game apart from a few achievements that I didn't get in my first playthrough (although I'll likely have soon if you're reading this in the future) and I'm going to tell you why I believe you should buy Hacknet. When I first bought Hacknet I wasn't really expected much, I mean it's just a clicking and typing game.. right? Well yes you do have the option to use a GUI to click, and primarily type out commands, however it surprised me how well made the game actually is. If you have never used a Linux system before, or Powershell on Windows, this game can actually teach you the basics as you move along in the game. It won't teach you how to actually hack or anything but it will teach you about basic commands used in Linux systems to this day. 

The game has a unique story with questionable morals for that matter. The rough of it is that a professional hacker has entrusted you with some very private information and teaches you the basics of hacking, then promptly disappears without much of a trace. As a hacker you complete contracts for different hacking scene groups and work your way up the hacking group ladders. It all has a climax too, and loads of unique easter eggs and secrets. 

The game does feature some bugs and annoyances, such as the clicking GUI sometimes seemingly not working or taking forever to actually process. But outside of that, it's a really well polished game. I wish I could buy it again for full price.

Don't expect this game to teach you about hacking, but the people behind Hacknet did an awesome job at finding a good balance between real-life hacking and with keeping the fun 'game' aspect. Real hacking is very complex and tedious so making a game out of it is certainly something that requires imagination and creativity, and the fact that Hacknet gives you an immersive sense of intelligence and power really makes me believe they've accomplished that balance.

Definitely recommend.

This is an extremely fun game, don't get me wrong, but I have two very major issues with it (especially the second one) that have prompted me to leave a negative review.  I very rarely review games on Steam, and only review the ones about which I am most passionately moved, positively or negatively.  In this case, negatively.  In contrast to my usual, I have enabled comments on this review -- feel free to state your feedback, whether you agree with me or not, just please remain respectful to me, the developers, other commenters, and anyone else as applicable.

There's a "TL;DR" at the end if you're lazy.

I'll start positive.  This game is crazy fun.  It is probably the funnest hacking-themed game I've ever played, and I've played a lot of them.  It was fun and helpful to see some things I recognize from real life, such as the default system port numbers being accurate and the existence of a few UNIX commands (my main OS has been FreeBSD for years, and my experience with UNIX helped with the gameplay in a way that felt good).  I liked seeing the C# source code and realizing it was actual, real C# source code that would probably work if the LESS_THAN was properly changed to a "<" sign, etc (C# is my main dev language, always a plus to see it referenced in a game at all).  That was cool, and I'll probably compile it later to have that tool on my PC for real (don't comment about the related real life security to this -- I assure you I already know, and it's just for fun).  The pacing was really good, and I got hooked fast.  So fast that I immediately bought the DLC, soundtrack, and DLC soundtrack for myself, then bought the game and DLC for both my wife and her boyfriend also.  Despite my negative review, I don't regret this decision at all, it's a very, very fun game.  Oh, the event thing that I can't discuss without giving spoilers, but well, the one where you need to get that thing back, that was super fun!  (Unimportant to the review and a spoiler:) I instinctively [spoiler]jumped to my host and forkbombed, apparently I was supposed to kill his forkbomb instead, oh well... I had already made a backup of that file just in case[/spoiler].  But anyway, the game was extremely fun, looks great, the music is great, and I'm excited to keep playing and see where things take me.

But there are two issues which were severe enough that they prompted me to leave a negative review despite all this.

The first issue isn't so bad and is easily rectified: This game is the pinnacle of Hollywood-style hacking.  It does it very well, and it references real hacking concepts in the game's flavor text and other areas.  Some tools are named the same as real ones, and you will probably learn a few real UNIX system port numbers, but that's about where the realism ends.  Oh, and [b]this wouldn't bother me in the slightest[/b] -- I love Hollywood-style hacking sim games! -- but it clearly says this in the "Features" section in the game's Steam page description, which to me is [u]blatant false advertisement[/u]:

[quote]
Real Hacking
Based on actual UNIX commands, Hacknet focuses on real hacking, not the Hollywood-style version of it.
[/quote]

If I stated what I consider my qualifications for knowing what constitutes "Hollywood-style" hacking, nobody would believe me, so I won't.  But even if you have never seen either a vtty or Hackers, I feel like anyone looking at the animation for the command called "porthack", god and the command name itself, and how it works, and everything related to the actual process of hacking (kinda the core concept in the entire game)... well I just think it doesn't take an expert to realize it's about as unrealistic as you can get.  If you don't believe me and this matters to you, buy the game and try it.  You will know I'm right within the 2 hour window to return it for a full refund, I assure you.  There is no "SSHCrack", no "FTPBounce", these wouldn't be PE executables if they did exist, PE doesn't even run on UNIX, "opening ports" and having requirements for a certain arbitrary number of open ports to "porthack" is very Hollywood.  Stahp.  Hollywood-style hacking is fine, don't be ashamed of it!  But most importantly, [b]advertise this game for it's many strengths, not for a falsehood[/b].  This game doesn't need lies to make it sound good, it's already a good game.  It's already a [i]great[/i] game.  Don't make false claims that sour its image.

Ok, now for the big one (to me).  Some people, many perhaps, won't care about this but I care.  I am quite literally sick to my stomach right now.  This has perhaps very minor spoilers for a very small number of optional (so far where I am in the story) missions, so I will spoiler-tag a lot to be safe, but even if you haven't played the game and hate spoilers, you probably won't be upset for reading the spoiler-tagged text in the next paragraph, it's the mildest of mild spoilers.

So, some of the missions require you to access a database of [spoiler]death row records[/spoiler] and modify them.  The missions are fine, and the topics are relevant.  I thought this was a positive thing to include in the game... until I gained access to this database and actually started reading the records.  I read about 40 of them in a row, unable to stop.  These were not made up, they were real records.  They had to be.  Surely the names were changed at least, right?  I Googled one at random and sure enough it was entirely real, and even the name, age, and date matched.  The [spoiler]last words[/spoiler] were their real [spoiler]last words[/spoiler], verbatim.  There is literally a massive database of actual real people's [spoiler]deaths[/spoiler] including their real [spoiler]last words[/spoiler] in the game, and there are missions to modify this database!  It is making light of a very serious topic with real people's real, actual names, turning it into a game.  If I am [spoiler]executed[/spoiler], I don't want my [spoiler]last words[/spoiler] to be made into a fun, "cool" game.  That's awful!  These families are mourning!  Please do not take real, actual tragedy and juxtapose it alongside comical IRC chat logs!  In a game?! I think my problem with this game is I'm a Linux nerd who's been working in IT for 15 years. I am clearly not the target audience. This game actually plays more like a text-based adventure game for people who know nothing about computers, but like the Hollywood idea of what a hacker is often portrayed as.

Despite what the store page says, this is one of the most [i]Hollywood[/i] hacking games I've ever played - it would be less Hollywood if it had the Universal Studios logo as an intro movie. Real "hacking" is nothing like this.

I'm not going to nitpick about how the commands or terminal don't behave exactly exactly like their *NIX counterparts. Plenty of other reviews have done that already in-depth. If you work in IT, use Linux unironically, or have even a basic level of networking knowledge, you will probably not like this game.

(Bonus points for anyone who got the [spoiler]Jurassic Park[/spoiler] reference)
This game has a 10/10 story. The gameplay is fun and captivating. Play this if you are interested in computers or anything close.

I think of Hacknet as a spiritual successor to Uplink, it has a good blend of fresh ideas and features borrowed from Uplink. When I compare the two, I view Hacknet as the more realistic game, whereas Uplink is more Hollywood styled. 

Hacknet features real Linux/UNIX commands, as well as real port numbers, Port 21 for FTP, Port 22 for SSH, 1433 for SQL etc. Now playing this won't teach you how to hack but it kind of gives you an idea of how it works, each system has a set number of ports that have to be open before you an crack it. Some of the later game systems have Proxy servers and Firewalls. Proxies can be overcome by opening a shell on 3-4 computers and telling them to spam it with junk traffic and data, meaning that it will allow unchecked traffic through, whereas Firewalls take a bit more time, you have to analyse it and doing so will reveal some characters, once you think you've got it you type SOLVE [FIREWALL SOLUTION] and it will check to see if it matches. 

Some tools can be run while a Proxy is up, but not while a Firewall is active and some can't be run with a Proxy active but they work while a Firewall is up. 
Each tool has it's own visual effect while it works and they're all beautifly done. My favorites being PortHack and SQL_Mem_Corrupt. 

The game is a bit more linear compared to Uplink, in Hacknet you're forced into the story as soon as the game begins, whereas with Uplink the story kicks in a couple of weeks into the game after some freelance work.

Hacknet has some intresting things to search for though, certain documents such as IRC logs are pretty funny. 

Overall though I'd say it's worth the buy, espiecally due to it getting a free multiplayer and some DLC content later in the year. And the soundtrack fits the game extremely well.

And for those who are intrested, the font used in the >HACKNET_ title can be found here: http://www.dafont.com/kremlin.font?text=HACKNET

Buy the DLC at your own peril...

Having just completed the main campaign at the time of writing - with an expansion DLC and community-made storylines to go grab whenever I fancy - I find myself applauding a demonstrable, confident and competent passion project.

Sitting at a fake operating system staring at flickering text and pondering what move to try next has no right to be this satisfying, yet Hacknet remains - with very few exceptions - a title that rewards ingenuity, curiosity and player agency. People say this is one of the definitive hacking simulators, and if this is indeed the case, it's not just the fact that you can screw around so intensively in a simulated internet ecosystem that you actually break the plot - it's because you're doing what hackers actually do most of the time, which is sit back, let out a big puffy-cheek sigh of mild exasperation and mutter "ugh, how do we get around THAT one?!" or "oh wow, I probably shouldn't have been able to do this yet am being rewarded for doing so."

The game teaches a few handy command line basics for those not in the know, but it's not going to give you much of anything in the way of dangerous IRL skills, largely because the premise of the game is that a fellow hacker has created a catch-all exploit that can open any computer like a can of sardines with the right complementary toolkit. Obtaining these tools, deepening your dive into the rabbithole and exploring a series of both serious and darkly comical scenarios is very much the crux of the game, and it's enjoyable and often tense in ways simply sitting at a computer has no right to be.

At the time of this review I have 10 hours in, and that's the core campaign done and dusted - enjoyable throughout and very rarely apt to let any pacing issues slip. Missions are unlocked by communicating with shady friends (and sometimes frenemies) who closely guard IP addresses and web tools that can expand your arsenal and uncover the truth behind those lurking in the darkest reaches of the web, trashing our rights man, TRAAAASHING.

Coupled with a banging soundtrack and just enough thrills and spills to make you sit up and pay attention when you get too cocky, Hacknet couples both careful thread-pulling at mysteries and intrigue with heartpounding oh-god-oh-dear-god panic moments where the screen goes weird and you know you're up a creek you were never invited to with a paddle your trembling fingers now can't spell the name of, just as you need it the most.

Excited to try community and DLC plotlines next!

Fun simulator and manual dexterity game with puzzle elements. You do not have to be a computer-whiz to enjoy Hacknet, but people comfortable at the command-line will enjoy it more. This game takes elements of computer system and makes a fun game out of them. For example, you don't have to know what program runs on the internet port 25, you just have to type that number at the end of the command.

The game simplifies the technical things and makes it fun, while leaving enough to make it also a challenge. It does a great job with the user interface, and I found everything very intuitive. I kept thinking of another hacking simulator, Uplink, and I think Hacknet does a better job with the game interface.

The gameplay was hit and miss for me. I felt like the game is not always consistent with the in-game logic. Find out a password, later it has changed. The commands are not always consistent (like "../filename" does not always work). Some commands are logged on servers but not others, and the purpose of server logs is not made clear. All these are minor issues, because the game is obviously going for fun not realism, but I wish the game did a better job informing me how the game world worked.

Hacknet is best when it feels like an open world, where every bit of information gathered could lead to a new story, when it is used in the right way. Unfortunately, most of the Hacknet stories are trails of breadcrumbs that lead from the email message to a server file, back to a workstation command, and finally a reply message of completion. And these stories can start to feel pretty repetitive, since most of the story time is spent hacking the server defenses, using the same weapon arsenal, each time.

All that said, the stories are well-written, even though most are short, including the primary Bit narrative. The game uses text assets to populate the game world to good effect. And there were just a few opportunities to figure things out independently, which made me feel pretty clever. You are half right, [b]most[/b] of these files are unimportant. There are decent puzzles in this game that happens in a specific scenario, but the contracts you get are pretty repetitive: [spoiler]probe the system, bypass proxy/firewall if those are there, open some ports, hack in, do your stuff, clear logs, get out[/spoiler]. Cool game if you're not familiar with Unix-based command-line usage, but seasoned Linux users will immediately realize the "genuine Linux commands" don't work like real Linux commands.  You can use "ls" but not "ls -l", you can run "cd /home" and then "ls" but not "ls /home" while in another directory, etc.  I kind of wish they implemented some of these commands more accurately, as they could have without modifying the gameplay/interaction.  I wasn't expecting the game to mirror a Unix-based OS and all of its behaviors, but it's just too far outside the realm of relatable in my personal opinion.  However, nonetheless, it's "hacking" in "Linux" with a fun interface, so it's kind of fun.  Definitely makes me want to fire up metasploit and relive my script kiddy days...

The game has a really cool and stylish UI, but for users who have been using Linux for a long time, it seems a bit "like a square peg in a round hole". I hope the game has more attention to detail. I use arch btw
